metadata.title: 贾湖骨笛 (Bone Flute from Jiahu)
metadata.period: Neolithic, Peiligang culture (c. 7000–5700 BC, site occupation range as listed)
metadata.object_type: Bone object · musical instrument (bone flute)
metadata.material: Wing bone (ulna) of red-crowned crane (Grus japonensis)
metadata.dimensions: c. 23 cm long, seven finger holes (sources give 23.1 cm and 23.6 cm)

works.short: Look closely at the small holes running along this flute. It was carved from the wing bone of a red-crowned crane, a bird whose bones are hard and hollow, which made them difficult to drill. Seven finger holes sit in a neat line along one side. Covering and opening them changes the pitch, so a player could move between notes using only the hands. The flute is about 23 centimetres long, small enough to rest in an adult's palm. It comes from Jiahu, a settlement in Wuyang, Henan Province, occupied during the early Neolithic Peiligang culture, roughly between 7000 and 5700 BC. It is among the oldest instruments of its kind, and it reminds us that music was being made in China millennia before the Shang dynasty. Look first, then imagine the sound it once made across a village.
works.expansion: Its sound is the subject of serious study. In 1999, a team of Chinese and American researchers reported tests on the best-preserved Jiahu flute, which they had played and analysed. They found that its seven holes could correspond to a scale remarkably close to the Western do-re-mi eight-note scale. That claim is striking, but it rests largely on one instrument and on modern interpretation of ancient sound, so specialists treat it as provisional. The flute's context is also debated. A Henan Museum online exhibition links this example to a tomb at Jiahu and suggests it was the one most cherished by the person buried there. Other accounts of the excavations do not mention a tomb, so that connection needs checking.
works.long:
Start with the material. This flute was made from the wing bone of a red-crowned crane. Crane bone is hard but hollow, which is a challenge for any toolmaker. It holds a shape well, yet a drill can easily split it. Surviving examples show small marks carved above and between the holes before drilling began, a sign that the spacing was worked out in advance rather than guessed.

Seven holes run in a straight line along one side. Covering and uncovering them with the fingers lets the player shift between pitches. Trial playing confirmed that the instrument is blown vertically, the same basic principle as many later flutes. Some accounts describe smaller holes beside the main seven that may have been used for tuning, but this detail comes from a single source, so treat it with care.

This example was found at Jiahu, a settlement in Wuyang County, Henan. The site was occupied during the Peiligang culture, roughly between 7000 and 5700 BC. Excavators have recovered more than thirty bone flutes there, most in fragments. According to the Henan Museum's online presentation, this flute was unearthed in 1987. Its three pieces show that it was broken and carefully mended in antiquity, so someone thought it worth keeping.

Here the story becomes debated. In 1999, researchers reported that the best-preserved Jiahu flute could be played and tonally analysed, and that its seven holes might correspond to a scale close to the Western do-re-mi eight-note scale. That is a remarkable result, but it depends heavily on one instrument and on modern interpretation of ancient sound.

We do not know what these flutes were for. Some researchers suspect ritual or ceremonial use, but the site does not reveal what tunes were played or who played them. Chinese myths recorded thousands of years later link flute playing with cranes, but whether that association existed at Jiahu is not known.

So why does this object matter today? It is one of the earliest known instruments that can still produce controlled, multi-note sounds. It shows that early farming communities in the Central Plains were already working with precise acoustics, shaping a hard material into an instrument that could be tuned by hand and played by ear. Look at it first as a made object, a piece of skilled craft. Then listen to it in your imagination.

metadata.title: 妇好鸮尊 (Owl-shaped Zun of Lady Fu Hao)
metadata.period: 商代晚期（约公元前13—前11世纪）; Late Shang dynasty, c. 13th–11th century BCE
metadata.object_type: 青铜器·酒器 (bronze ritual wine vessel, zun in the form of an owl)
metadata.material: Bronze (青铜)
metadata.dimensions: 通高46.3 cm (overall height); 口长16.4 cm (mouth length); weight 16 kg, per the Henan Museum record

works.short: Look first at the head. Two small ears rise from a high crown, the eyes are round, the beak is broad, and the wings are folded tight against the body. This is an owl, cast in bronze in the late Shang dynasty, around 1200 BCE, and it is a ritual wine vessel. Notice how it stands. Its strong legs and broad, drooping tail meet the ground at three points, so the tail does structural work rather than merely decorating the piece. Now bend toward the rim. Just below the mouth, on the inner wall, two characters are cast: 妇好, Fu Hao. That inscription links the vessel to Fu Hao, a consort of King Wu Ding, whose tomb was excavated at Yinxu near Anyang in 1976. Roughly 3,200 years later, the owl still stands on its three points.
works.expansion: The surface is as striking as the silhouette. Nearly every part is covered in thunder pattern, leiwen, 雷纹, a fine ground that gives the bronze a dense, textured look. Over it, cicadas appear on the beak and chest, a double-headed kui dragon, 夔, sits on each side of the neck, and coiled snakes curl near the wings. Taotie masks, the mysterious beast faces typical of Shang bronzes, appear among them. The result is busy, yet the owl’s outline stays clear. Curators at the museum describe the bird as sacred and linked to bravery and victory. One scholar has argued that it represents a war god, but that is an interpretation, not a settled fact. The pair also matters: the other owl is in the National Museum of China in Beijing, and the two were shown together in Henan for the first time.
works.long:
Start with the silhouette. This is an owl, rendered in bronze more than three thousand years ago, and it stands on three points: two thick legs and a broad, drooping tail that meets the ground as firmly as the feet. Look at the head. A high crown rises above small ears, the eyes are round, and the beak is wide. The wings are folded tightly against the sides, so the bird seems both still and alert. That tension between stillness and watchfulness is what makes the piece feel alive.

It is a zun, a ritual wine vessel. Shang bronzes of this kind were used in ritual settings, and the bird’s body is the container itself, with an opening at the top. The animal form and the working vessel are one object.

The surface is dense. Almost all of it is covered in thunder pattern, leiwen, 雷纹, a fine ground that makes the bronze look textured. Over that ground, cicadas appear on the beak and chest, double-headed kui dragons, 夔, sit on the neck, and taotie masks and coiled snakes appear elsewhere on the body. The museum describes the overall style as dignified and fierce, yet the owl’s outline stays clear.

Then look just below the mouth, on the inside of the vessel. Two characters are cast there: 妇好, Fu Hao. The inscription identifies the owner. Fu Hao was a consort of King Wu Ding, and her tomb was excavated in 1976 at Yinxu, the late Shang capital near modern Anyang. The tomb was undisturbed when found and held hundreds of bronzes. Oracle bone inscriptions also name her as a military leader.

Why an owl? Curators at the museum describe the bird as sacred and link it to bravery and victory. One scholar has gone further and argued that the owl was a war-god symbol, but that reading is an interpretation rather than a settled fact. Owls also carried different reputations in later Chinese history, so their meaning should not be assumed to stay fixed.

Finally, this is one of a pair. The other owl is in the National Museum of China in Beijing, and the two were shown together in Henan for the first time in a recent exhibition. Whether you stand before one owl or two, the question is the same: how did Shang workers make an animal look so watchful?

metadata.title: 莲鹤方壶 (Lianhe Fanghu, Square Hu with Lotus and Crane)
metadata.period: Spring and Autumn period (春秋时期), late phase, roughly 6th century BCE (770–476 BCE per secondary sources; not confirmed against the official record)
metadata.object_type: Bronze wine vessel (青铜器·盛酒器), hu type; some sources say wine or water
metadata.material: Bronze (青铜)

works.short: Begin at the top. On the lid, a crane stands with its wings spread, as if about to take flight, and two tiers of lotus petals open around it. The petals are pierced with many tiny holes, so the lid is worked almost like lace. Now follow the eye down the body. The vessel is square in section, with a rectangular mouth, a long neck, and a belly that swells and then tapers toward the base. Dragons climb its corners, heads turned back over their shoulders, and creatures crouch beneath the foot to bear its weight. This is a hu, a vessel for holding wine or another liquid. It was cast in bronze around the sixth century BCE, in the late Spring and Autumn period, when Zhou royal authority was weakening. Notice how every line in the design rises toward the crane.
works.expansion: The story of this vessel begins underground. In 1923, digging at Lijialou, near Xinzheng in Henan, uncovered bronzes from a large tomb traditionally linked to the rulers of Zheng, a small state of the period. The occupant has not been securely identified; scholars have proposed a few Zheng dukes, and the question remains open. Burial matters here. In a tomb, bronzes of this scale signaled the rank of the person buried there, but the record does not fully reveal how such a vessel was used while the living held it. The lotus and crane are commonly read as symbols of purity and longevity. That reading is plausible, yet it is an interpretation, not a documented intention. The Henan Museum holds one of a pair. The twin was separated long ago, and today the other sits in Beijing, at the Palace Museum.
works.long:
Start with the crane. Standing on the lid of this bronze, it has its wings spread as if about to lift off, and it rises from two tiers of lotus petals that open outward like a flower in bloom. The petals are pierced with many small holes, so the lid is a delicate openwork frame rather than a solid cap. Now look at the body. It is square in section, with a rectangular mouth, a long neck, and a belly that swells and tapers toward the foot. Dragons climb its corners with their heads turned back, and mythical creatures crouch beneath the base to support its weight. The whole thing is cast in bronze, and it is heavy. Some sources give its weight as about 64 kilograms, but published measurements vary, so treat the exact figures as provisional.

This is a hu, a vessel for holding wine or another liquid. Its shape suggests it was made for pouring, and its scale suggests it was meant to impress. It was cast during the late Spring and Autumn period, roughly the sixth century BCE, when the Zhou royal house still held nominal authority but regional states such as Zheng were asserting their own power. Bronzes of this size and finish were a statement of rank.

The vessel was found in 1923, in a field at Lijialou near Xinzheng, Henan, in what was traditionally identified as a tomb of the Zheng rulers. Finding it in a tomb tells us where it ended up, but the record does not fully reveal how it was used while the living held it. The occupant of that tomb has not been securely identified, and scholars have proposed a few Zheng dukes. The pair was later divided. One vessel is here in Zhengzhou, and the other is in Beijing's Palace Museum.

The scholar Guo Moruo gave it the name Lianhe fanghu, the lotus-and-crane square hu. The name captures the two motifs that define the design. The lotus and crane are often read as symbols of purity and longevity, a reading that is plausible but reflects later interpretation rather than a documented intention. What we can say with more confidence is that the lid, the body, and the dragons were designed as one composition, with the crane as its focal point. Pay attention to it, and you will see how nearly every line leads upward toward it.

metadata.title: 武则天金简 (Wu Zetian Gold Slip)
metadata.period: Tang dynasty, Wu Zhou period (武周); inscription dated 7 July 700 CE (Jiushi 1st year, 久视元年)
metadata.object_type: 金器·祭祀铭文 (gold ritual slip with inscription)
metadata.material: Gold alloy: about 90% gold and 10% silver per a 2008 museum test as reported; one China Daily advertorial gives over 96% gold
metadata.dimensions: 36.2 cm long, 8 cm wide, about 0.1 cm thick; 223.5 g (press reports; not checked against the museum record)

works.short: Start with the material. This narrow strip of gold, about thirty-six centimetres long, is covered in more than sixty characters, and it was never meant for a display case. It is a petition. Around the year 700, Wu Zetian, the only woman to rule China as emperor, sent a Daoist envoy to Mount Song in Henan with this slip. Its message asks the celestial authorities to pardon the empress's wrongdoings. Look at the surface and you will see the characters were not stamped but cut into the metal by hand, one stroke at a time. Earlier slips of this kind were made of jade, silver or bronze, so this is the first known gold example. Read the lines slowly, and you are reading a personal request, issued in the empress's own name, meant for the gods.
works.expansion: Now look at how it was made. The gold was hammered into a sheet only about a millimetre thick, and the characters were incised as outlines, each stroke drawn with a pair of parallel lines, a technique called double-line writing. The surface was then burnished smooth. The metal is not pure gold. A 2008 test by the Henan Museum found roughly ninety percent gold and ten percent silver, a proportion reported as typical of Tang gold, though another published figure gives higher purity, so the exact composition is still open. The strip survived by chance. In 1982, a young farmer on Junji Peak, a summit of Mount Song, took it for pastry wrapping. Only after he wiped away the dirt did he see the writing. A dealer offered him 100,000 yuan, and he handed the slip to the state instead.
works.long:
Picture a sheet of gold, long and narrow, that you could hold in one hand. It looks like an ornament, but it was never meant for a display case. This is a petition, and its author was an empress.

Wu Zetian is the only woman in Chinese history to rule as emperor. She founded her own Zhou dynasty, which interrupted the Tang for about fifteen years. In the year 700, the inscription tells us, she sent a Daoist envoy named Hu Chao to Mount Song, one of China's five sacred mountains. He was to leave the slip there, asking the Three Officials and the Nine Bureaus, the celestial authorities in Daoist belief, to pardon her wrongdoings. The text is dated the seventh day of the seventh month.

The wording is short but deliberate. Five of its characters were ones Wu Zetian had created herself, including 曌, the character she devised for her own name. That suggests a personal hand in the wording, although the record names Hu Chao as the envoy who submitted it. The slip was first nicknamed after its supposed purpose, the removal of the empress's sins, and that label still shapes how people read it.

Here the debate begins. The word for sin could mean a moral failing, but it could also refer to suffering, such as illness. Some writers link the slip to an illness the empress is recorded as having around that time, and to pills Hu Chao had made for her. That reading is an inference, not something the inscription says outright. Later researchers tend to read the slip as a prayer for blessing and protection.

Whatever the precise motive, the object shows a ruler at the height of her power turning to the mountains and the gods, and choosing gold to do it. Whether you read it as a confession, a plea, or a prayer for health, the slip carries a voice that official histories rarely give us: a sovereign asking, in her own careful language, for forgiveness.

metadata.title: 云纹铜禁 (Bronze Jin Stand with Cloud Pattern)
metadata.period: Late Spring and Autumn period (春秋晚期); cast no later than 552 BC, according to the excavation evidence
metadata.object_type: Bronze ritual wine stand (jin 禁, 承酒器)
metadata.material: Bronze (青铜)
metadata.dimensions: Overall height 28.8 cm; body length 103 cm; width 46 cm; weight 95.5 kg (Henan Museum record)

works.short: Start with the top, because that is where your eye goes first. What looks like a solid tray turns out to be a lattice of cast cloud scrolls, pierced so you can see through to the hollow frame below. This is a jin, a bronze stand built to hold a wine vessel. It dates to the late Spring and Autumn period, around the sixth century BC, and was made for the Chu state, whose tombs at Xichuan in Henan have yielded this piece. Twelve dragon-shaped beasts cling to the sides of the frame, their open jaws and extended tongues turned toward the center. Twelve more beasts sit beneath and carry the load. The whole piece is about 29 centimeters tall, yet it weighs roughly 95 kilograms. Few bronzes manage to be this heavy and this delicate at once.
works.expansion: The stand also raises a question about how it was made. The museum's record calls it one of the earliest Chinese bronzes cast by the lost-wax method. In that process, the form is modeled in wax, coated in clay, and the wax is melted out, leaving a cavity that molten bronze fills. Many scholars place the arrival of lost-wax casting in China much later, and often connect it with India. If this stand was truly lost-wax cast, the technique would be far older than the early Tang texts usually cited for it. Other researchers doubt that Bronze Age workshops used the method at all. They argue the stand was assembled from separately molded pieces joined by welding. The debate remains open. Either way, its makers controlled molten metal across a large and intricately pierced form, which is a remarkable achievement in itself.
works.long:
Lift your eyes to the top of this bronze. What looks like a solid tray is really a lattice of cloud scrolls, pierced so you can look straight through them to the hollow frame beneath. The whole piece is about 29 centimeters tall and weighs roughly 95 kilograms, and nearly all of that mass rests on twelve beasts crouched under the frame.

It is a jin, a stand made to hold a wine vessel. The word is usually read as "prohibition," and a long-standing explanation links the name to the Zhou view that excessive drinking had doomed the Xia and Shang dynasties. That is a traditional explanation, not something the object itself proves. What the object does show is how carefully its makers handled wine. Twelve dragon-shaped beasts cling to its sides, their open mouths turned toward the center and their tongues extended. Some other accounts describe the lower beasts as tiger-like, but the museum's record calls them dragons.

The stand comes from the Chu state in the late Spring and Autumn period. It was found at Xiasi, in Xichuan county, Nanyang, Henan, and the official record dates its casting to no later than 552 BC. Local bronzes first came to light in 1977, when a drought lowered the water in the Danjiangkou reservoir. The tomb owner is commonly identified as Zi Geng, also called Prince Wuzi, a chief minister of Chu. That identification rests mainly on inscriptions on a set of ding cauldrons from the same tomb, not on the stand itself.

The bigger question is how it was cast. The museum describes it as one of the earliest Chinese bronzes made by lost-wax casting, a method in which a wax model is coated in clay and melted away to leave a cavity for molten bronze. If that is right, the technique would be far older than the Tang-dynasty texts that are usually cited for it. Many scholars instead place the arrival of lost-wax casting in China much later and connect it with India. Others doubt that the Bronze Age used the method at all, and argue that the stand was assembled from separately molded pieces joined by welding. The debate remains open.

Whichever way it was made, the stand shows a workshop able to control molten metal across a large and intricately pierced form.

metadata.title: 杜岭方鼎 (Duling Square Ding)
metadata.period: Early Shang dynasty (商代早期); the list gives c. 16th–15th century BCE, and secondary sources give a wider range of c. 1590–1300 BCE
metadata.object_type: Bronze ritual vessel (青铜器·礼器), a square ding
metadata.material: Bronze (青铜)
metadata.dimensions: Overall height 87 cm; mouth about 61 cm square; ear height 17 cm; foot height 25.5 cm; weight about 64.25 kg

works.short: Walk slowly around this bronze and begin with its corners. The body is square, with straight walls and a flat rim, and it stands on four hollow legs. It is a ding, a ritual vessel of the Shang dynasty used to hold food at ceremonies. This example is about 87 centimeters tall and weighs roughly 64 kilograms, so even empty it is a heavy object. It dates to the early Shang period, around 3,400 years ago. Look at the upper belly, where a fierce face called a taotie stares out of the bronze. Along the sides and lower body, small raised knobs, known as nipple bosses, break up the surface. Their purpose is debated, but their orderly placement shows how carefully the surface was planned. You are looking at the smaller of a pair of dings found together in Zhengzhou in 1974.
works.expansion: Here is a question this vessel leaves open: why was something this heavy put into the ground? In September 1974, workers digging a tunnel on the Duling mound in Zhengzhou came upon it about six meters down. The mound sits roughly 300 meters outside the western wall of the early Shang city, which is one reason the find matters to historians studying how that city grew. The vessel did not come alone. A larger square ding, about a meter tall and now in the National Museum of China, was found with it, and a cattle skeleton lay among the remains. Some archaeologists have suggested that the group may have been linked to ritual sacrifice, but that idea is a hypothesis, not a proven fact. What the find does establish is the scale of the effort. Two dings this heavy required enormous quantities of metal and organized labor, whatever the reason for their deposit.
works.long:
Start with the corners. This bronze is built like a box rather than a bowl. Its body is square, its walls rise straight to a flat rim, and two upright ears stand on that rim. Underneath, four hollow cylindrical legs lift the vessel off the ground. The Chinese name for this type is ding, a ritual vessel used in the Shang dynasty to hold food offered during ceremonies.

This is the Duling square ding, made in the early Shang period, around 3,400 years ago. It stands about 87 centimeters high, its mouth measures roughly 61 centimeters on each side, and it weighs about 64 kilograms. Shang bronze was cast in sections of clay mould that were then assembled, and a vessel this size needed a large quantity of metal and many skilled, coordinated workers.

Look at the decoration. The upper belly carries a taotie, a fierce mask with staring eyes, a motif that appears across Shang bronzes. Small raised knobs called nipple bosses cover the sides and lower body, breaking up the surface in an ordered pattern. Scholars debate what the taotie represented, and the purpose of the knobs is also uncertain. What is clear is that the surface was planned with care, so the vessel rewards a slow walk around it.

Its discovery is as remarkable as its form. In September 1974, workers digging a tunnel on the Duling mound in Zhengzhou reached two square dings about six meters underground. The mound sits roughly 300 meters outside the western wall of the early Shang city. The larger of the pair, about a meter tall, is now in the National Museum of China. This smaller one is held by the Henan Museum. Accounts of who first spotted the vessels differ.

That setting raises the question of purpose. A cattle skeleton was found together with the pair, and some archaeologists have suggested that the group may have been connected to royal sacrifice. That remains a hypothesis, not a settled conclusion. The find also feeds a larger debate about Zhengzhou itself. Scholars still argue about which early Shang ruler, if any, held court here, so the vessel is evidence in an argument that is still open.

Whatever its exact role, the Duling ding shows how far Shang bronze-casting had come. Circle it slowly, and notice how the square corners sharpen the whole form.
research_flags: Official record found on the Henan Museum site (chnmus.net, 镇院之宝 column) with title, date, dimensions and weight, but no accession number; accession_number left null.
Dating: the list says c. 16th–15th century BCE; secondary sources give c. 1590–1300 BCE. Scripts say 'early Shang' and 'around 3,400 years ago' to stay within both.

Record confusion: the Henan Museum page gives the Duling No. 1 height as both 87 and 100 cm. Other sources say No. 1 (100 cm, 86.4 kg) is held by the National Museum of China and No. 2 (87 cm, about 64.25 kg) is the Henan Museum piece, which matches the list.

Discoverer disputed: one account credits a sanitation worker, Yuan Haijun, who later claimed the find in 2010, while another says unnamed workers. Location names also vary (Zhangzhai South/Front Street, Duling Street).
Sacrifice link: the cattle skeleton is reported, but the royal sacrifice connection is only Yang Yubin's suggestion, presented as a hypothesis.
Zhengzhou's identity as an early Shang capital and the king it belonged to are disputed; the scripts say so briefly.

The record's superlatives (earliest, largest, most perfectly cast) are not supported by evidence in the sources and are not used. Its 'nine' versus 'ten' treasure ranking is inconsistent and not used.
Casting method: piece-mould casting is described as the general Shang practice. No technical study specific to this vessel was found, so the script attributes it to Shang casting generally.
Taotie and nipple-boss meanings are presented as open to debate, not as settled symbolism.

metadata.title: 玉柄铁剑 (Jade-Hilted Iron Sword)
metadata.period: Western Zhou dynasty, late period (西周晚期, c. 8th century BCE); the museum record gives 西周
metadata.object_type: Jade and iron weapon (玉器、铁器·兵器)
metadata.material: Iron blade; bronze core with turquoise inlay; Hetian nephrite jade hilt (和田青玉)
metadata.dimensions: Overall length 34.2 cm; hilt length 12.2 cm (blade length of about 22 cm appears in a secondary source only)

works.short: Start with the hilt, because it holds the surprise. It looks like a solid jade handle, but it is an assembly. Two hollow sections of greenish nephrite, cut from Hetian jade in China's far west, slide together over a bronze core, and small copper pins lock them in place. Turquoise strips are set into the bronze and into the top of the pommel. Now look at the blade. It is iron, and iron was far rarer than bronze in Western Zhou China. The blade is forged onto the bronze core, so the three materials meet in one continuous object. This sword came from tomb M2001 at the Guo state cemetery in Sanmenxia, Henan, excavated in 1990. Iron, bronze, and jade together make a weapon that was meant to impress as much as to fight.
works.expansion: The blade is where the sword earns its place in history. Analysis by researchers at the University of Science and Technology Beijing identified the iron as bloomery carburized steel, meaning it was smelted and worked by people rather than taken from a meteorite. If that reading holds, this is among the earliest scientifically confirmed examples of artificial iron in China, and it pushes the country's iron history back by more than a century. Scholars are cautious, though. Some suggest the blade, hilt, and core were made separately and joined with lacquer, but that idea has not been tested scientifically. Ask yourself why a weapon with such costly parts was buried in a Guo lord's tomb. Prestige is the most likely answer, but the sword's exact meaning remains open.
works.long:
Most visitors notice the jade first, and they are right to. The handle is made of greenish nephrite, the stone known as Hetian jade, carved into two hollow sections that slide together over a bronze core. Look closely and you will see thin strips of turquoise set into the bronze and the top of the pommel. The fit is careful rather than showy. Copper pins pass through small holes on each side to lock the parts together, so the jade is held mechanically rather than hidden under decoration.

The blade is the real surprise. It is iron, forged onto the bronze core, and it came from tomb M2001 at the Guo state cemetery in Sanmenxia, Henan, excavated in 1990. Guo was a Western Zhou state, and this tomb is linked to a Guo lord known as Guo Ji. In the late Western Zhou, bronze carried the prestige. Ritual vessels and weapons for the powerful were typically cast in bronze, while iron was far scarcer. A sword with an iron blade in a lord's tomb therefore stands out.

Analysis of the blade, reported by researchers at the University of Science and Technology Beijing, identified it as bloomery carburized steel, a product of artificial smelting rather than meteorite iron. If that identification holds, the sword is one of the earliest scientifically confirmed examples of iron made by human hands in China, and it pushes the country's iron history back by more than a century. Scholars are careful here, however. The cemetery's chronology is still debated, and the cemetery as a whole runs from the late Western Zhou into the early Spring and Autumn period. Some researchers also suggest the blade, hilt, and bronze core were made separately and joined with lacquer, an idea not yet tested in a laboratory.

What does the sword mean? The combination of materials suggests it was meant to advertise rank as much as to fight. It may have signaled the political and military power of its owner, but that reading is an interpretation, not a documented fact. What is certain is that the object brings stone, copper, and iron into one weapon, and asks you to consider which of them the owner valued most.
research_flags: Period: the brief says 西周晚期 (c. 8th century BCE); the official record says only 西周. The cemetery as a whole is described as spanning late Western Zhou into early Spring and Autumn, so the date is not settled.
Accession number not found in the official record or any source checked.
Sanmenxia Guo State Museum is said to display the sword, while the official record says it is held by Henan Museum. Display or loan status is unverified.

The iron analysis (USTB, bloomery carburized steel, 'earliest scientifically confirmed' artificial iron, pushing back more than a century) rests on a popular article. The primary report was not located, and the priority claim is contested in the wider literature.
Lacquer-joining hypothesis for blade and hilt is reported as untested (PKU paper).
Attribution of tomb M2001 to Guo Ji (虢季) is as reported by sources; the relationship between Guo Ji and Guo Zhong is unclear.
Symbolism (political and military power) is an interpretation only.
Blade length of about 22 cm appears only in a secondary source; the record gives overall length 34.2 cm and hilt length 12.2 cm.

metadata.title: 四神云气图壁画 (Four Spirits and Clouds Mural)
metadata.period: Early Western Han dynasty (西汉早期), c. 2nd century BCE; listed date consistent with the sources checked
metadata.object_type: 墓葬壁画 (tomb mural)
metadata.material: Mineral pigments (cinnabar red, white, green, black) on plaster; mural cut out in its original form and transferred to the museum
metadata.dimensions: Approx. 514 x 327 cm (16.8 m²) per Chinese-language sources; 550 x 350 cm per a China Daily page presented with Henan Museum. Not confirmed against the museum record.

works.short: Look up at this painting. It was made for the ceiling of a royal tomb chamber, and its ground is a deep cinnabar red, a mineral pigment made from mercury sulphide. Out of that red field a great dragon coils through the centre, while a vermilion bird hovers above and a white tiger crouches below. Painted clouds fill the spaces between them, so the whole scene reads as a sky. These animals are the four directional creatures of Chinese cosmology, which give the mural its title, Four Spirits and Clouds. Made in the early Western Han dynasty, around the second century BCE, it is described by museum sources as one of the earliest and largest tomb murals found in China. Its survival is remarkable: the painted plaster was carefully cut from its tomb and brought to Henan Museum, where it is displayed today.
works.expansion: This mural was never meant to decorate a house or a temple. It belonged to a royal tomb of the Liang kingdom, a Western Han state ruled by princes of the Liu family, whose burial was cut into the rock of Mangdang Mountain near Yongcheng in Henan. Museum accounts link the tomb to King Gong of Liang, Liu Mai, but other sources name King Xiao, and some name no occupant at all, so the identity is still disputed. The tomb's design made such painting possible. One account describes a shift in royal tombs from vertical shaft graves to horizontal cave chambers, which gave painters more wall and ceiling space. The mural is painted in red, white, green and black pigments on plaster, and because it covers a ceiling, visitors inside the chamber would have looked straight up at it.
works.long:
Begin with the ceiling. A painting like this is easy to picture on a wall, but this one was laid across the top of a burial chamber, so anyone standing inside the royal tomb would have looked straight up into it. The ground is a deep cinnabar red, made from a mineral pigment that gives the whole field its warmth. Out of that red emerge the four directional creatures of Chinese cosmology. A dragon, its body twisting through the centre, dominates the scene, its tongue curling around a strange hybrid beast. Above it a vermilion bird, the guardian of the south, pecks at one of the dragon's horns, while below a white tiger holds a long flower in its mouth. The fourth figure is usually identified as the Black Tortoise, though its form does not match that creature neatly, and scholars have not fully settled the question. Painted clouds fill the gaps among the animals, so the whole composition reads as a sky.

Setting matters as much as the image. The tomb belonged to the Liang kingdom, a Western Han state ruled by princes of the Liu family, and it was cut into the rock of Mangdang Mountain near Yongcheng in Henan. Museum accounts associate the tomb with King Gong of Liang, Liu Mai, but other sources name King Xiao, and some name no occupant at all. That uncertainty matters, because the identity of the person buried here shapes how we read the painting's rank and purpose. The dating to the early Western Han, around the second century BCE, is consistent across the sources I checked. The image itself was painted with mineral pigments in red, white, green and black on plaster.

Its survival is the other story. In the late 1980s the painted plaster was carefully cut out in its original form and transferred to the Henan Museum, where it now stands among the institution's celebrated treasures. Museum publications describe it as one of the earliest and largest tomb murals found in China. Standing before it, you are looking at a painted sky that was once sealed underground, and that now survives where visitors can study it at close range.
research_flags: Official Henan Museum collection record not reachable (henanmuseum.com not on allowlist); accession number and official URL unverified, set to null.
Occupant disputed: Liu Mai, King Gong of Liang (most sources, incl. China Daily page presented with Henan Museum); Liang King Xiao (梁孝王) in one baijiahao article; occupant unnamed in another.
Tomb location disputed: Shiyuan tomb (柿园墓), Mangdang Mountain; China Daily page says Baoanshan, Yongcheng.
Excavation year conflicts: 1986 (Henan Daily) vs 1987 (baijiahao); script says late 1980s.
Dimensions conflict: 514 x 327 cm (Chinese sources) vs 550 x 350 cm (China Daily/Henan Museum page) and Google Arts record (327 x 514 cm, 'Henan Provincial Museum'); unresolved.
Fourth creature unidentified: sources say Black Tortoise (玄武) or 'mythical beast'; hybrid form does not match the conventional Black Tortoise; script hedges.
Claims of 'earliest and largest' tomb mural are museum/press superlatives, not independently verified.
Alamy caption links a 'Liu Fa tomb' four-spirits image; not corroborated and likely unrelated, disregarded.
Mural cut out and moved in 1980s/1990s per sources; exact transfer date and method not confirmed by an official record.

metadata.title: 汝窑天蓝釉刻花鹅颈瓶 (Ru Ware Sky-Blue Glazed Carved Goose-Neck Vase)
metadata.period: Northern Song dynasty (北宋, 960-1127 per museum record; list says 11th-12th century)
metadata.object_type: Ceramic (瓷器); display vessel (陈设器) per list, not stated in museum record
metadata.material: Ru ware porcelain (瓷器) with sky-blue glaze over greyish-buff body (香灰色胎); glaze composition not recorded
metadata.dimensions: Height 19.5 cm; mouth diameter 5.6 cm; foot diameter 8.2 cm (museum record)

works.short: Let the color reach you first. This slender vase is covered in a sky-blue glaze, clear and glossy, the shade of a sky after rain. It is a Ru ware piece from the Northern Song dynasty, standing just under twenty centimetres tall. Its outline is a gentle S-curve: a flared mouth, a long thin neck, and a rounded belly above a small foot. Look closely at the neck and belly. Sprays of lotus are carved into the body, but they do not sit on the surface. They show faintly beneath the blue, appearing and fading as the light shifts. Chinese connoisseurs prized this shade most highly, and only a few sky-blue Ru pieces survive. This one was excavated in 1987 at Qingliangsi village in Baofeng County, Henan. Give it a slow look, and it rewards you.
works.expansion: Now turn the vase over, because the foot holds a clue to how it was made. The base is bare of glaze, and the clay beneath has a greyish tone, with fine grains of sand stuck to it. Those grains suggest the vase was fired standing on small supports rather than directly on the kiln floor. Potters usually left the foot unglazed, since glaze would fuse to whatever it touched. Look at the surface too. A fine web of crackle spreads evenly across the glaze, catching the light in a pattern of hairline lines. Then comes the harder question: when was it made? Estimates for the kiln's active years range from roughly 1086 to 1125, and specialists still debate the exact span. Some link the kiln to the reign of Emperor Huizong, though that connection remains open to discussion. Keep that uncertainty in mind as you look at the blue.
works.long:
Start with the color, because it is what most visitors notice first. The glaze over this vase is a clear, pale sky-blue, even and glossy, the shade that Chinese connoisseurs once called the most precious of all. This is Ru ware, a porcelain made at the Qingliangsi kiln in what is now Baofeng County, Henan, during the Northern Song dynasty. The vase is a Ru official-kiln piece, and its outline is a relaxed S-curve: a flared mouth, a long slender neck, a rounded belly and a small foot. Look carefully at the neck and belly. Sprays of lotus, carved into the body, show faintly through the glaze, as though the design floats beneath the surface and appears only when light moves across it. Museum text says this hidden lotus design is not seen on transmitted Ru pieces.

Turn it over and the story becomes technical. The foot ring is bare of glaze, the clay beneath is greyish, and tiny grains of sand cling to it. Those grains show the vase was fired standing on small supports rather than directly on the kiln floor. Such traces are how specialists reconstruct the work of the potters who made it.

The kiln behind the vase was a court enterprise. Ru ware is often described as perhaps the first official ware commissioned by the imperial court. Most accounts say the finest pieces were kept for the palace, and only rejected pieces reached a wider market. Its productive life was brief. Estimates of how long it operated range from about twenty to about forty years, and most tie its output to the reign of Emperor Huizong. Scholars still debate the exact dates, and production is generally linked to the upheavals of the 1120s.

This vase was not found in a tomb or a palace. It was excavated in 1987 at the kiln site itself, in Qingliangsi village. We do not know who handled it or where it stood. One scholarly study groups goose-neck vases among display wares, which suggests a decorative role, but its original use is not recorded and should not be assumed.

Its importance today lies in its rarity. Only a small number of sky-blue Ru pieces are known from collections, and the museum counts this one among its nine treasures. Its color, shape and hidden carving reward patient looking. Take your time with it.
research_flags: Title: list says 汝窑天蓝釉刻花鹅颈瓶; the museum's 藏品精粹 page matches this. A second museum page (chnmus.net, 镇院之宝 series) calls it 汝官窑天蓝釉刻花鹅颈瓶.

Accession number: not found. Neither museum page gives a 编号/藏品号. Official_record URL is the 藏品精粹 page on chnmus.net (河南博物院 site), not a confirmed registration record. henanmuseum.com was not reachable.
Mouth diameter: museum page gives 口径5.6 cm; maigoo.com gives 5.9 cm. Script uses height only, so no conflict in audio, but the record value is 5.6 cm.

Excavation: 1987 at Qingliangsi village, Baofeng County is consistent across sources; thepaper.cn says excavations ran 1987-1989 and that a separate complete washer was found in 1986. Script says 1987 only.

Material: list says porcelain, but the museum record only files it under 瓷器 and describes a greyish-buff body (香灰色胎) and sky-blue glaze; glaze composition not stated. Object type 陈设器 is from the list; the record does not state it. Original use is not recorded; display-ware classification is one scholarly article's grouping (Huang & Hai, 2014).

Dating: list gives 11-12th c.; record gives 北宋 (960-1127). Kiln operating span disputed: about 20 years (Henan government), 1086-1106 (Sotheby's), c.1107-1125 (Rawson), about 40 years (Vainker). Attribution to Huizong's reign is common but not settled.

Claims to treat as museum or promotional, not verified fact: 'unseen among transmitted Ru pieces' and 'the only sky-blue piece from the excavation' or 'only carved one among five' (Henan government and press). The record calls it one of the museum's nine treasures. Headline 'worth over 100 million' and 'only one in the world' are unsupported.
Decoration: record says two groups of 折枝莲花 (lotus sprigs) on neck and belly, faint under the glaze. The 'only complete' wording applies to a 1986 washer, not clearly to this vase.

metadata.title: 彩陶双连壶 (Painted Pottery Double-Linked Vessel)
metadata.period: Neolithic, Yangshao culture (新石器时代·仰韶文化); date as listed c. 3500–3000 BCE, not stated in the record
metadata.object_type: Painted pottery drinking vessel (彩陶·饮酒器), as described in the record; list says 彩陶·生活器
metadata.material: Fine-paste red earthenware (泥质红陶) with black painted decoration over a red slip (红衣黑彩)
metadata.dimensions: Height 20.1 cm, base diameter 5 cm (per record)

works.short: Look closely at this vessel and you are looking at two jars joined at the belly. It is a painted double-linked jar from the Yangshao culture, unearthed in 1972 at Dahecun, a Neolithic site in Zhengzhou. The two bodies are nearly identical, set side by side and connected by an oval opening. The surface is fine red earthenware, covered with black painted bands of parallel lines and clusters of short strokes. Archaeologists first found the two halves separated, then realised they fitted together exactly. The museum reads it as a drinking vessel for shared ceremonies: two people could each hold one body and drink at the same moment. Standing about twenty centimetres tall, it is small enough for two hands, and its form seems built around sharing.
works.expansion: The painted pattern rewards a second look. The black marks come in two arrangements: long horizontal bands, and groups of three short strokes, drawn upright on one body and slanted on the other. Some researchers suggest the difference stands for two separate groups, perhaps two communities brought together. A former director of the Dahecun site museum has offered a version of this reading, in which rival groups reconciled by drinking from the same vessel. It is a compelling story, but it remains an interpretation, and the pottery carries no text that confirms it. The Chinese cross-cup wine toast, jiaobei jiu (交杯酒), is sometimes mentioned alongside the vessel, but scholars have not established any direct link. What the evidence firmly supports is the craft: two bodies of almost identical shape, joined and painted with a controlled design that has survived more than five thousand years underground.
works.long:
Start by looking at the shape. What appears to be one jar is in fact two, rising side by side from a shared base and joined at the belly by an oval opening. Each body mirrors the other, and the whole piece stands just over twenty centimetres tall, small enough to hold in two hands. This is a painted double-linked jar of the Yangshao culture, the Neolithic tradition that flourished along the middle Yellow River. Its fine red earthenware was coated with a red slip and decorated in black: coarse horizontal lines, and groups of short strokes, some drawn upright and some slanted.

Its discovery is part of its story. It was unearthed in 1972 at Dahecun, a settlement site in Zhengzhou. The two halves were found apart. Only when they were reconstructed did archaeologists see that they fitted together exactly, which suggests the two bodies were made as a matched pair.

So what was it for? The Henan Museum reads it as a drinking vessel, perhaps used on ceremonial occasions, in which two people each held one body and drank at the same moment. That reading fits the design, since the shared opening links the two sides into a single object. Some researchers go further, proposing that the contrast between upright and slanted marks stands for two different groups, and that the vessel marked a pact between them. It is an appealing idea, but it is an interpretation. No inscription on the pot confirms it, and later practices such as the cross-cup wine toast are sometimes linked to vessels like this without proof.

What the evidence firmly supports is the craftsmanship. Shaping two matching bodies, joining them, and applying an even black pattern across curved surfaces demanded real skill with clay and fire.

It matters today because it asks a question that pottery can only partly answer: how did people in the Neolithic mark a shared bond? This vessel offers a clue, not a full answer, and that is exactly why it rewards careful looking.
research_flags: Title matches the list (彩陶双连壶). Record gives 1972 excavation at Dahecun (大河村遗址), Zhengzhou.
Object type differs: list says 彩陶·生活器 (daily-life vessel); the Henan Museum record describes it as a 饮酒器 (drinking vessel) used on important ceremonial occasions. Record used.
Dimensions: record says height 20.1 cm, base 5 cm; a 2024 press article gives height 20 cm and mouth diameter 6.4 cm. Record used.

Date c. 3500–3000 BCE comes from the list only. The record gives no years, and I found no dating source confirming it. Scripts use 'more than five thousand years' to stay within the range. Verify before publishing.
Accession number not found on the record page; the page also does not state the current collection unit explicitly, though it credits 河南博物院. henanmuseum.com was not reachable.

Use as a drinking vessel for alliance or shared-oath rites is scholarly interpretation, not proven. The 'clan strokes' reading is attributed to a former Dahecun museum director and is flagged as interpretation. A press legend linking the vessel to the Yan and Huang emperors was excluded as unsupported.
Link to cross-cup wine (交杯酒) and minority customs is unproven per the record's own caveat; scripts say so.

metadata.title: 王子午鼎 (Ding of Prince Ziwu, Wangzi Wu ding)
metadata.period: Spring and Autumn period (770-476 BC)
metadata.object_type: Bronze ritual vessel (ding, tripod cauldron)
metadata.material: Bronze
metadata.dimensions: Height 49 cm; mouth diameter 58.3 cm (sources conflict; see research_flags)

works.short: Start with the shape. This bronze is a ding, a tripod vessel used to cook meat for sacrifice, and its heavy body rests on three legs. The Ding of Prince Ziwu was made in the Spring and Autumn period for the Chu kingdom, a powerful southern state whose bronze style developed its own character. What makes it stand out is its inscription. Cast inside the vessel, the text runs to more than eighty characters, unusually long for a ritual cauldron. It says the ding was made for ancestral sacrifices and for ceremonies that sealed alliances. Measure it against your own height: at just under half a meter tall, it is a substantial pot. Picture it on an ancestral altar, steaming with meat, and you begin to understand why a cauldron could carry so much weight.
works.expansion: Now turn to where it was found. In 1978, excavators opened a Chu tomb at Xiasi, in Xichuan county, Nanyang, in southwestern Henan. Today that landscape lies within the Danjiang reservoir area of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project, a reminder of how much history can sit beneath modern engineering. The inscription names the maker as Prince Ziwu, and the museum's account links him to a son of King Zhuang of Chu. That attribution is traditional, so it is worth holding loosely. Some accounts also describe a set of seven ding of the same shape in graded sizes, though sources disagree on that count. Finally, one scholarly account notes that the inscription uses bird-and-worm script, a decorative style more often seen on weapons.
works.long:
Imagine a cauldron that could cook a sacrificial meal and, at the same time, announce who had commissioned it. That is the Ding of Prince Ziwu, one of the most important bronzes from the southern kingdom of Chu. Start with its shape. It is a ding, a tripod vessel with a lid and three legs, the kind of cooking pot used in Shang and Zhou ritual. Its body stands just under half a meter high, roughly 49 centimeters, and measures about 58 centimeters across the mouth, which would have made it a serious object to lift and to fill.

Ding were not kitchen equipment in the ordinary sense. Meat cooked in them was offered to the ancestors, and scholars generally link the number and size of ding a family owned to its rank. This one is an unusually ambitious example. Its inscription, cast inside the vessel, runs to more than eighty characters. As the museum describes it, the text records that the ding was cast for ancestral sacrifices and for ceremonies that sealed alliances. It also claims that the maker's benevolent rule has earned the love and respect of the people of Chu.

The vessel dates to the Spring and Autumn period, when Chu, a large state along the middle Yangtze and Han rivers, was expanding and developing a bronze style of its own. Prince Ziwu is traditionally identified as a son of King Zhuang of Chu, an attribution worth holding loosely.

The ding was excavated in 1978 from a tomb at Xiasi in Xichuan county, Nanyang, in southwestern Henan. Today the site lies within the Danjiang reservoir area, part of the South-to-North Water Diversion Project, so the find is a reminder of how much history can sit beneath modern engineering. Some accounts report that the tomb held a set of seven ding of the same shape in graded sizes, but the exact count, and the number of characters in the inscription, are given differently in different sources.

The inscription is also written in bird-and-worm script, a decorative style that one scholarly account notes is more often found on short weapon inscriptions than on vessels like this. Seeing it today, you are looking at a cooking pot designed to speak as much as to feed.

Metadata comes from a China Daily page carrying a Henan Museum copyright line and a 2022 China Daily article calling the ding a Henan Museum permanent treasure.

metadata.title: 王孙诰编钟 (Wangsun Gao Bell Set)
metadata.period: Spring and Autumn period (春秋), roughly the 6th century BCE
metadata.object_type: Bronze percussion instrument: bell set (编钟), 26 yong bells (甬钟)
metadata.material: Bronze

works.short: Before you stands a set of twenty-six bronze bells, each made to be struck and each made to sing. Archaeologists call them yong bells, after the hollow stem on top. What makes this set remarkable is that every bell sounds two pitches, depending on where it is struck. According to the Henan Museum, striking the front and side areas together produces a harmonious third. Across the set, the range spans about four and a half octaves. The museum calls it the largest and most numerous Spring and Autumn bell set yet found in China. It came from a Chu tomb at Xichuan in Henan, excavated in 1978. Listen for the two voices in each bell, and you begin to hear what these bells were built to do.
works.expansion: The bells carry an inscription, which the museum records as 113 characters. It names the maker as Wang Sun Gao, and says the bells were made to delight the king of Chu, honored guests, fathers and elder brothers, and officers, for ten thousand years. Those words point to ceremony and feasting, the settings the museum associates with this kind of music. But the inscription is contested. A recent online essay by a single author argues that its text was copied from a bell now in San Francisco, and that the characters were added in modern times. That essay is unfinished and has not been peer reviewed, and it does not claim the bells themselves are fake. Treat the name Wang Sun Gao as the museum's reading, and the question as still open.
works.long:
Look first at the number. Twenty-six bronze bells, each a yong bell named for the hollow stem on its top. Visitors tend to stop at the shapes, but the real story is in the sound. According to the Henan Museum, each bell is cast to sound two pitches, one from its front face and one from its side, and striking both together produces a harmonious third. Across the set, the range spans about four and a half octaves. For a sixth-century BCE instrument, that is a remarkable span, and it explains why the museum describes the set as the largest, most numerous, and best-sounding bell set of the Spring and Autumn period so far found in China. Those are the museum's own superlatives, and they rest on the instruments themselves.

The bells were excavated in 1978 from a tomb at Xiasi, in Xichuan county, Henan. The tomb is a Chu tomb. Chu was a southern state whose core lay in the middle Yangzi region, and its bronzes and musical habits differ in character from those of the northern courts. Bell sets like this one were markers of rank, and the number of bells and their range signaled how important their owner was. The museum says this set was played in ritual and banquet settings.

The bells also carry an inscription of 113 characters. It names the maker as Wang Sun Gao and says the bells were made to delight the king of Chu, honored guests, fathers and elder brothers, and officers, for ten thousand years. Those words suggest a public world of ceremony and feasting, where the music was meant to be heard by many people.

But the inscription is contested. A recent online essay by a single author argues that its text was copied from a bell now in San Francisco, and that the characters were added in modern times. That essay is unfinished and has not been peer reviewed, and it does not claim the bells themselves are fake. Scholars also debate who owned the tomb. The name Wang Sun Gao and the identity of the owner therefore remain open questions.

So look at the set as a working instrument, one that was designed to be played. The maker's name may be disputed, but the sound the bells were built to make is not.

metadata.title: 牛尊 (Ox-shaped zun, bronze wine vessel)
metadata.period: Late Shang dynasty (商代晚期), c. 13th–11th century BCE, as listed; not confirmed by a Henan Museum record
metadata.object_type: Bronze ritual wine vessel (青铜器·酒器), zun
metadata.material: Bronze (青铜)
metadata.dimensions: Approx. 22.5 cm high, 40 cm long, 7.1 kg (single secondary source; unverified)
metadata.museum: Henan Museum (河南博物院) - NOT CONFIRMED; see research_flags

works.short: Look first at the head. This bronze ox, made in Late Shang China about three thousand years ago, stands on short, sturdy legs. Two upright horns crown its head, its mouth sits slightly open, and its tail hangs low. Despite its animal form, it is a wine vessel, a zun, the kind of container used in ritual drinking. The whole body is the container. A lid covers an opening on the animal's back, and the surface is crowded with tigers, birds, fish and dragons. Turn your attention to the walls, which are only about three millimetres thick in most places. Casting a hollow animal of this size, with its horns and legs intact, took real control from the foundry workers who made it. It shows how Shang craftsmen turned a living creature into an instrument of ritual.
works.expansion: Look closer and you will find a name. Inside the lid and on the neck, the bronze carries the inscription Ya Chang, 亚长. Archaeologists connect that name with the large tomb where the vessel was found at Huayuanzhuang, in the Yinxu area of Anyang, the last capital of the Shang. Read carefully, the bronze is less an anonymous container than a document that ties one name to one tomb. Who Ya Chang was remains debated. The character ya is often read as a rank or title in Shang inscriptions, so the vessel may record an official rather than a simple owner. The animal is also disputed. Most people call it an ox or bull, but many scholars link bronzes of this type to the xi (兕), a powerful animal named in oracle-bone inscriptions and possibly a water buffalo.
works.long:
Start with the head. Two upright horns rise above a broad face, the ears sit close, the legs are short and sturdy, and the tail droops down the back. The animal stands about twenty-two centimetres high, yet it was made to hold wine. Zun is the general term for the ritual wine vessels used in Shang ceremonies, and a vessel of this kind signalled rank among the people who used it. Its neck has an internal partition that helps control the flow of liquid from the mouth, a small technical detail that shows how carefully the maker thought about pouring.

Look at the body next. The bronze is cast remarkably thin, only about three millimetres in most places, and it is covered in dense decoration. A phoenix sits below the ear, tigers flank the belly, and dragons, birds and fish fill the rest. Casting an animal this complex in one piece, with thin walls and a lid that fits over an opening on the back, demanded great control of the mould and the metal. Modern researchers have reconstructed its casting and cooling process, which shows how much had to go right in the foundry.

The vessel also carries a name. The inscription Ya Chang is cast inside the lid and on the neck. The vessel was found in a large tomb at Huayuanzhuang, in the Yinxu area of Anyang, the last capital of the Shang. Scholars are careful about what the name tells us. The character ya is often read as a title or rank, and it is not clear whether Chang was a personal name, a lineage name, or both. Press accounts describe Ya Chang as a military general or a tribal leader, but those labels are interpretations, not settled facts.

The animal itself is also debated. It is often described as an ox or bull, but many scholars connect bronzes of this type to the xi (兕), a powerful creature named in oracle-bone inscriptions and possibly a water buffalo. Whatever it was, the bronze turns an everyday ritual drink into a reminder of how power, animal and ancestor were bound together.

metadata.title: 金缕玉衣 (Jade Burial Suit with Gold Thread)
metadata.period: Western Han dynasty (西汉), per Henan Museum jade feature; catalogue range listed as 汉代 (206 BCE–220 CE) not independently verified
metadata.object_type: 玉器·葬服 (jade; funerary burial garment)
metadata.material: jade plaques (2,008 pieces per Henan Museum account), joined with gold wire

works.short: Look closely at this burial suit and you will see that it is not carved from a single stone. It is made of 2,008 separate jade plaques, most of them a deep blue-green, joined together with fine gold wire. Its Chinese name, 金缕玉衣, jīnlǚ yùyī, means "jade garment with gold thread." Makers shaped each plaque and stitched them into a body-shaped garment in five parts: a head covering, a jacket, trouser legs, hands and feet. The plaques differ in size, shape and colour, fitted to follow the head, limbs and joints. The gold thread holds the whole structure together. Han-period jade suits were funerary garments for emperors and senior nobles, made to protect the body after death. This example was excavated in 1985 from a Western Han tomb at Xishan, in Yongcheng, Henan. Look at the joins, where the making is most visible.
works.expansion: Look at the small objects too. The Henan Museum account lists a jade pig to be held in the hand, a jade cicada placed in the mouth, and jade plugs for the ears and nose. The cicada is often read as a symbol of rebirth, but that is an interpretation, not an inscription, and scholars read the pig differently. Together these pieces show that the suit was meant to work as part of a complete burial set, not as clothing alone. The owner is also debated. Some accounts tie this tomb to the Liang kingdom, a princely state in this region, and others name a particular prince. Neither identification has been confirmed. Much of what we know about who was buried here depends on what excavators recorded at the time.
works.long:
Begin with the colour. Where you might expect a single carved figure, you find a garment built from 2,008 separate jade plaques, most of them a deep blue-green, with others in lighter and darker tones. Each plaque is a small piece of shaped jade, and together they cover the head, the jacket, the trousers, the hands and the feet. The plaques are joined with gold wire that passes through holes in each piece and holds the whole structure together. The suit was made to fit a human body, and it still keeps that shape.

Its Chinese name, 金缕玉衣, jīnlǚ yùyī, means jade garment with gold thread. The thread matters. Han tombs also produced suits joined with silver or silk, and the choice of thread is generally read as a sign of rank. Gold was the costliest of these materials.

The suit was a funerary garment. Museum accounts describe such suits as burial garments for Han emperors and senior nobles, made to protect the body after death. Some sources add that the jade was believed to help the deceased reach immortality. That is a belief about the afterlife, not a demonstrated outcome, so it is best held as a belief. Its job was to protect the body.

Look also at the small objects that accompanied the suit. The Henan Museum account lists a jade pig to be held in the hand, a jade cicada placed in the mouth, and jade plugs for the ears and nose. The cicada is often read as a symbol of rebirth, but that reading is an interpretation rather than something written on the object. Scholars have offered different views on the pig.

This suit was excavated in 1985 from a Western Han tomb at Xishan, in Yongcheng, Henan. Its owner is not secure. Some accounts link the tomb to the Liang kingdom, a princely state in this region, and some name a particular prince. Neither identification has been confirmed in the sources I could consult, so the person who wore the suit remains uncertain.

Why does it deserve attention today? It shows the labour and wealth a princely family could direct toward the afterlife, and the problem of fitting hard stone to the shape of a human body. Stand close, follow one gold join from plaque to plaque, and you can see the engineering that holds an entire garment together.

metadata.title: 三彩角形杯 (Sancai Horn-Shaped Cup)
metadata.period: Tang dynasty (唐代, 618–907)
metadata.object_type: Sancai horn-shaped cup (drinking-vessel form); burial object (明器, mingqi) per museum record
metadata.material: Earthenware (陶器) with three-colour (sancai) glaze of yellow, green and white over the whole body
metadata.dimensions: Length 14 cm, height 7.0 cm, mouth diameter 7.0 cm

works.short: Start with the head. At the upper end of this curved, horn-shaped cup, an animal turns its head back over its shoulder, a flower sprig held in its beak. That sprig becomes the handle. Now look at the surface. Yellow, green and white glazes flow over the whole body, and scrolling grass patterns wind across it. The shape travelled a long way to get here. Horn-shaped drinking vessels, called lai tong (来通) in Chinese, trace back to Greek rhyta and reached China along the Silk Road. Tang craftsmen took that foreign silhouette and dressed it in their own colours. At about fourteen centimetres long, it fits in one hand. Some visitors see a peacock, which gave the cup its nickname. Others read a dragon. The museum treats both readings as open, so decide for yourself.
works.expansion: Now consider where it was found and why it was made. In 1976, excavators at Houwangzhuang, on the western outskirts of Zhengzhou, recovered this cup. The museum classifies it as a mingqi (明器), a burial object made to accompany the dead. It was a grave good, not a piece for the dinner table. The museum dates it to the Tang and compares it with pieces from tombs of the Gaozong and Zhongzong reigns, roughly the later seventh to early eighth century. Sancai glazes are typically lead-based, which is why the colours sit so softly on the earthenware body. Compare it with a small bird-shaped rhyton in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, made in the seventh or eighth century. It shows the same basic idea: a foreign drinking vessel reworked in Tang glaze.
works.long:
Pick the cup up with your eyes first. It is curved like a horn, about fourteen centimetres long and seven centimetres high, with an oval mouth at the wide end. Near the top, an animal turns its head back over its shoulder, a flower sprig held in its beak, and that sprig forms the handle. The whole earthenware body is covered in yellow, green and white glaze, with scrolling grass patterns winding across it. The colours are bright and the scale is intimate. It was made to sit comfortably in the hand.

The silhouette is the real story. Horn-shaped drinking vessels, known in Chinese as lai tong (来通), trace back to the Greek rhyton, and they reached China along the Silk Road during the Northern and Southern Dynasties. Chinese potters took that foreign form and rebuilt it in their own clay and glazes. The result looks foreign at a glance and Chinese on closer inspection, and that mix is what makes it worth a second look.

The head is the most debated detail. Many people see a peacock, and that reading gave the cup its nickname, the peacock cup. The museum also considers a dragon's head equally possible and leaves the question open. It is a useful reminder that an animal on a Tang object does not carry one fixed meaning. Treat the head as a question rather than an answer.

Its purpose is more certain. The museum classifies it as a mingqi (明器), a burial object made to accompany the dead. It was not made for everyday drinking, even though its shape suggests a drinking vessel. It was excavated in 1976 at Houwangzhuang, on the western outskirts of Zhengzhou in Henan. The museum compares it with cups from tombs of the Gaozong and Zhongzong reigns, which places such pieces roughly in the later seventh and early eighth centuries. The dating rests on that comparison, because the cup itself carries only the broad label Tang.

So why does it deserve attention today? In one small vessel you can see the Tang world's appetite for foreign shapes and its confidence in remaking them. Look at the grass scrolls and the turned head, and you are looking at a Chinese answer to a Greek idea.

metadata.title: 绿釉陶立狗 (Standing Dog with Green Glaze, translation by this guide)
metadata.period: Han dynasty, 206 BCE–220 CE (per the item list; Western or Eastern Han not verified)
metadata.object_type: Pottery, mingqi (burial object) (per the item list: 陶器·明器)
metadata.material: Earthenware with green glaze (from the title; glaze composition not verified)

works.short:
Start with the posture. This dog stands upright on four legs, and its body is covered in a glossy green glaze that gives plain clay a bright, glassy finish. The title, 绿釉陶立狗, tells you the essentials: green glaze, pottery, and a dog standing up.

But this is not a pet to be walked. It is a mingqi, or 明器, often translated as "spirit utensil." Such pieces were made for tombs rather than homes. Han families placed models of animals, household goods, and everyday life in graves, so the dead would have what they needed in the afterlife. A dog was among the most familiar of those companions, and its role was simple: to keep its owner company in the next world.

The glaze does much of the decorative work, and the upright stance does the rest.
works.expansion:
Why would a family spend on a glazed figure rather than leave a plain one? In the Han dynasty, burial goods were no longer reserved for emperors and nobles alone. As government service spread to a wider class of officials, more households could afford to furnish a tomb with models of the life they hoped to continue. Clay made this possible: it was plentiful, easy to shape, and suited everything from rough earthenware to glazed pieces.

The green glaze is the other half of the story. Han green glazes were typically lead-based, fused in the kiln into a glassy coating. Glazing set certain pieces apart from plain earthenware.

A word of caution. Whether this particular figure uses a lead glaze, and where and when it was buried, has not yet been confirmed against the museum's own record.
works.long:
Most visitors would take a figure like this for a toy or a decorative animal. Look closer. Its title, 绿釉陶立狗, describes a dog standing upright, made of pottery and covered in a green glaze. Those few characters point to a whole way of thinking about death in the Han dynasty, which lasted from 206 BCE to 220 CE.

The dog is a mingqi, or 明器, often translated as "spirit utensil." The term refers to objects made for burial rather than daily use. Han families placed in their tombs replicas of what the deceased had known in life: farm buildings, livestock, household tools, and attendants. The models were meant to supply the soul with what it needed. A dog, one of the most familiar companions in a household, was a natural member of that group. Its role in the tomb was to keep its owner company in the next world.

Making such figures was economical. Clay was abundant and easy to shape, so it could serve families across a wide social range. What set some pieces apart was glaze. Han green glazes were typically lead-based, applied to the surface and fired until they formed a bright, glassy skin over the earthenware. The glaze gave the figure a richer appearance than plain pottery, even though it was made from the same humble clay.

Who buried such objects? The Han period saw power spread beyond the emperor and the aristocracy. As government service reached a broader class of officials, more households could afford to furnish a tomb in this way. Tomb goods became a way of signalling status and securing comfort in death, and a glazed model of a dog could express both loyalty and a family's means.

We should be careful here. The record for this particular piece has not yet been checked against the museum's collection data, so its precise date within the Han, its findspot, and whether its glaze is lead-based all remain to be confirmed. What we can say with confidence is that it belongs to a tradition in which everyday animals and objects, shaped in clay, were given a second life underground.

That is perhaps the most affecting thing about it. A companion that was familiar in life was modelled again in clay and glaze, so that its company could continue into the afterlife.

metadata.title: 四神画像陶灶 (Pottery Stove with Four Spirits Decoration)
metadata.period: Han dynasty (汉代), per a secondary source; Eastern Han (东汉, 25–220 CE) per task list, not independently verified
metadata.object_type: 陶器·明器 (pottery; burial object), per task list
metadata.material: Pottery (陶; fired clay)

works.short: Look closely at the small clay stove in front of you. It was never meant to cook a meal. Han tomb builders placed miniature household goods, called míngqì (明器), or spirit articles, in tombs so the dead would be provided for in the afterlife. This model kitchen, with its cooking holes and smoke vent, is one such provision. What sets it apart is the decoration pressed into its surface. The Four Spirits, the Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird and Black Tortoise, guarded the four directions of the sky. Here, a Black Tortoise, or Xuanwu (玄武), is molded on either side of the stove door, and a Vermilion Bird decorates the back wall. Find them, then imagine the cook these guardians were meant to protect.
works.expansion: Now look at the rest of the stove. The decoration goes beyond the four directions. Above the door, an eagle is molded into the clay. On the side walls, a winged figure rides a dragon, and a warrior fights a tiger. Fish appear on the sides of the cooking top. Their meaning is open to interpretation. Some scholars relate such imagery to ideas of ascent and immortality, while others focus on the stove's everyday role. The practical details are clear enough. Two fire holes hold cauldrons, and a round vent beside them drew smoke away from the cook. Han households are known to have honored a Stove God, 灶神, near the hearth, so cooking here may have carried spiritual meaning too. Whether this stove was made with that deity in mind cannot be proven.
works.long: Begin with the front. Between two molded creatures, a small semicircular opening leads into the firebox, and on either side of it a Black Tortoise, or Xuanwu (玄武), is pressed into the clay. Now picture a working kitchen from the Han period. A fire would have burned beneath cauldrons set into the cooking top, and a vent would have carried smoke away from the cook. This model copies that everyday object closely, with two fire holes and a round smoke vent beside them. Yet it was not made for cooking. Han tombs held miniature household goods, called míngqì (明器), or spirit articles, made so the dead would be supplied in the afterlife, much as the living were. A model kitchen was a way of making sure the dead would never go hungry. The Four Spirits, the Azure Dragon, White Tiger, Vermilion Bird and Black Tortoise, guarded the four directions, and by the Han they were a common way of picturing the sky and the space around a building. The Black Tortoise appears by the door, and the Vermilion Bird is placed on the back wall, opposite the entrance. The designer does not stop at the four animals, however. The side walls show a winged figure riding a dragon and a warrior fighting a tiger. An eagle is molded above the door, and fish decorate the cooking top. Their meaning is open to interpretation. Some scholars relate imagery of ascent and immortality to scenes like these, while others focus on the stove's everyday role. Han households are known to have honored a Stove God, 灶神, near the hearth, so the cooking space carried spiritual meaning as well as practical use. Whether this stove was made with that deity in mind cannot be proven. What makes the object worth attention is the way it turns a kitchen into a small cosmos. Whoever made it did not simply reproduce a stove. Look again at the guardians around the door, then at the cauldron holes, and you are seeing a household's hope for the next world, fired in clay.
