metadata.title: 父乙角 (Fù Yǐ Jué: bronze jue wine vessel of "Father Yi")
metadata.period: Early Western Zhou (西周早期); the museum record gives no year range
metadata.object_type: Bronze wine vessel (青铜酒器), jue type (角)
metadata.material: Bronze (青铜)
metadata.dimensions: Overall height 29 cm; mouth length 20.3 cm; mouth width 9.8 cm

works.short: Start with the lid. This bronze wine vessel from Henan Museum has a lid shaped like a roof ridge, topped by a small half-ring knob. On one side of the body, a half-ring handle ends in an animal head. Now look at the surface. Many bronzes of this age are crusted green, but this one is nearly black and glossy, close to old lacquer, with almost no corrosion. Three triangular feet lift the body, though one of them is a later replacement. Twelve characters are cast on the lid and twelve on the body, and the two texts match. They record a dedication to a father called 父乙, Fù Yǐ, which translates roughly as Father Yi. The inscription calls the vessel a precious ritual vessel. Its surface is decorated with animal faces, dragons, and cloud-and-thunder patterns, all packed into a small space.
works.expansion: Now look at the inscription as a pair. The same twelve characters appear on the lid and on the body, so the two halves carry one message. That message is a dedication to a father named 父乙, and it calls the vessel a precious ritual vessel. The repetition matters because it makes the lid part of the inscribed object, not merely a cover. Then look at the feet. The replacement foot sits directly beneath the animal-headed handle. It tells you this vessel has a history after it was cast, because a part was replaced at some point, though the sources do not say when or by whom. Read the vessel as a document, not just a shape, and the feet become part of the story.
works.long:
Stand in front of this bronze wine vessel and start with its colour. Most bronzes of this age have turned green or crusty after millennia in the ground. This one is almost black and glossy, with barely any corrosion. The museum compares its surface to old black lacquer and notes that such a surface is uncommon among Shang and Zhou bronzes.

It is a jue, a type of wine vessel, about 29 centimeters tall. The lid rises into a shape like a roof ridge. The body flares at the mouth, pinches inward at the waist, and rests on three triangular feet. On one side, a half-ring handle ends in an animal head. Every section is decorated with animal faces, triangular patterns, dragons, and a cloud-and-thunder ground pattern, with raised ridges along the edges. The museum describes the decorative method as a three-layer technique, which suggests how the designs were built up in layers. One of the three feet, the museum notes, is a later replacement.

The most revealing part is the inscription. Twelve characters are cast on the lid and twelve on the body, and they match. Read together, they record a dedication to a father named 父乙, usually rendered Father Yi, and they describe the vessel as a precious ritual vessel. That wording ties the object to ancestral worship from the early Western Zhou, roughly three thousand years ago. The sources do not say how the vessel was used in ritual, so it is wise not to fill that gap with guesses.

Its history is also unusual. In 1986, a group of fourteen bronzes was recovered from river silt near Xinyang, in southern Henan. A second, nearly identical cup was found with this one, and the museum holds this example. That near-twin matters, because it shows that the vessels were made as a set and then came out of the ground together.

Why does it deserve attention today? Because it can be read, not just admired. Its dark surface, its twelve matching characters, and its one replaced foot each tell a different part of its story. Look at it slowly, and it becomes a record of who it honoured and how carefully it was made.

metadata.title: 三彩狮形座枕 (Sancai Lion-Shaped Pillow with Base)
metadata.period: 宋 (Song dynasty), as recorded by the museum; 960–1279 is the dynastic span, not from the record
metadata.object_type: 瓷器 (ceramics), the museum's category; list says 陶瓷·生活器

works.short: Look at this object as a pillow first. Its title, 三彩狮形座枕, names a lion-shaped form on a base, and a pillow is a headrest, so whatever the lion looks like, its job was to support a sleeping head. The Henan Museum dates it to the Song dynasty, which lasted from 960 to 1279. Next, consider the word 三彩, sancai, which literally means three colours. It is a loose label. Scholars note that Song-period wares carrying this name are generally multicolour, low-temperature lead-glazed pieces, and the number three is not a count. As you walk around the lion, let the glaze, not the number, guide your attention. Notice how a sculpted animal becomes an everyday bedding object, serious in its form yet made for something as quiet as a night's sleep.
works.expansion: The title's word, sancai, deserves a closer look, because the museum record does not settle how this piece should be described. Chinese scholars have long used the phrase Song sancai for multicolour wares of the Song period, yet one specialist study calls that usage imprecise and treats these wares as low-temperature lead-glazed objects. The museum files this one under ceramics, a broad category that does not say whether the body is porcelain or earthenware. The distinction is not pedantic. Lead glazes are fired at lower temperatures than porcelain glazes, so the body and surface tell different stories about how the piece was made. Until a material description is available, treat the body and glaze as open questions, and let your own eyes check the surface against the label.
works.long:
Start with the most basic fact about this object: it is a pillow, made to be slept on. Its title, 三彩狮形座枕, describes a lion-shaped form resting on a 座, a stand or base. The Henan Museum dates it to the Song dynasty, which lasted from 960 to 1279, and files it among its ceramics.

The word 三彩 needs care. It literally means three colours, but scholars point out that the label is applied loosely to Song-period wares. One specialist study describes these pieces as multicolour, low-temperature lead-glazed objects, and treats the name Song sancai as an imprecise habit. The number three is not a count. Think of the name as a family resemblance rather than a precise recipe.

The official record is also sparse. It gives the title, the period and the category, but not the dimensions, a material description, excavation details or a maker, so this guide will not supply them. Nor should we assume a meaning for the lion. The motif appears across Chinese art in Buddhist settings, imperial contexts and everyday objects, and its significance shifts with each. Without evidence from this piece's original setting, the safest reading is the simplest one.

That simple reading is useful. Notice how little it needs: no legend, no ritual, just a bed and a head. A pillow is a headrest, so the lion's form had to serve a sleeping head. The sculpted animal was not a figure standing beside a bed. It was the bed object itself, with enough weight and stability to hold the head through a night's rest. Imagine the object in use, and the decorative and the practical begin to fuse. That combination, a lion turned into something quiet and domestic, is what makes this pillow worth attention. Look at it as a tool first and a sculpture second, and its details will start to reveal how people actually lived with ceramics.

metadata.title: 白釉莲瓣碗 (White-glazed lotus-petal bowl)
metadata.period: Liao dynasty (辽代), 916–1125, per the task list; not confirmed against the museum record
metadata.object_type: Ceramics, daily-use vessel (瓷器·生活器), per the task list; not confirmed against the museum record
metadata.material: Ceramic with white glaze, per the task list; clay body not verified

works.short: Look at the wall of this bowl and you will find petals. Its sides are shaped like the petals of a lotus (莲瓣), each one swelling outward and curving back toward the foot, so a plain working bowl takes on the look of a half-open flower. The white glaze is worth noticing too. The bowl belongs to the Liao dynasty, the state founded by the Khitan people in the north, which governed a mixed population of Khitan, Han Chinese and others. Lotus motifs had a long life in Chinese art, most famously in Buddhist settings, but on an everyday bowl they may have been chiefly decorative. This was made to be used, washed and used again. Notice how the petals catch the light as you walk around it, and how their simple repetition gives the bowl its calm rhythm.
works.expansion: Here is a question that has no settled answer: where was this bowl made? Liao territory covered much of northern China, Inner Mongolia and Manchuria, and its kilns produced white wares. Yet this bowl is in Henan, in the Central Plains, far south of the Liao heartland, and that distance sharpens the question. Scholars often connect Liao white porcelain with northern centers such as Ding in Hebei. They think white porcelain forms and techniques passed from these northern kilns to neighboring kilns during the Liao and Jin periods. So a bowl like this one may come from a Liao workshop, from a Ding-linked kiln, or from somewhere in between. Attribution here is a matter of evidence and argument. Treat the question as part of the bowl's story, because the answer changes what it tells us about how northern ceramic skills traveled.
works.long:
Begin with the wall beneath the rim. Run your eye around this bowl and you find a rhythm of petal-like forms, each one swelling outward and folding back toward the foot, until the whole vessel reads as a flower that has half opened. It is a simple thing to hold: a bowl for everyday use, made to be washed and used again. The lotus, though, has a long history in Chinese art. It rose to prominence through Buddhist temple decoration in the Tang period, and by the time this bowl was made, lotus petals were among the most familiar motifs on ceramics. A motif does not carry one fixed meaning from one century to the next, however. On a working bowl the petals may have been chiefly pleasing to the eye, or they may have carried a Buddhist resonance for the person who used it.

The glaze matters as much as the shape. White-glazed wares were a notable part of ceramic production in the north during the Liao dynasty, which lasted from the early tenth century to 1125. The Khitan people who founded Liao came from the steppe, and they governed a large population of Han Chinese farmers, artisans and officials. The state drew on the skills of older Central Plains workshops, and scholars often link Liao white porcelain to Ding, the famous kiln in Hebei. Ding forms and techniques seem to have passed to neighboring kilns during the Liao and Jin periods, so a bowl like this one belongs to a wider northern conversation about clay, glaze and taste.

That conversation also raises a question about this particular bowl. It is now in a museum in Henan, in the Central Plains far south of the Liao heartland. Was it made by a Liao workshop, by a kiln connected to Ding, or somewhere in between? Scholars weigh such questions against evidence. The answer shapes what the bowl tells us about how northern skills traveled.

What, finally, does it reveal? A plain bowl from a northern state, shaped by a mixed population and by a long Buddhist and Chinese inheritance, shows how far these cultures had learned from one another. Its type points toward everyday use rather than court display, and it asks us to give a humble form real care. That is why it deserves a slow look today.
